title: Just Three Types
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. names three basic patterns teachers fall into as the school year winds down: Limping Mode (a burnout-driven survival slog he's personally hit at the end of his third year and again in spring 2023), Striving Mode (an intensity-driven push to accomplish everything, which he associates with his early career years and two Teacher of the Year finalist years), and the Focused Finish, a deliberately narrow approach where a teacher picks one to three high-impact experiments to run between March and year's end rather than trying to do everything or coasting. He argues the Focused Finish outperforms both extremes because it retains the sense of purpose that Limping Mode lacks while respecting the limited bandwidth that Striving Mode ignores, and credits it as a meaningful part of why he's still teaching. Stuart closes by inviting readers to identify which of the three patterns describes their own typical end-of-year approach and previews a follow-up tool for identifying a personal Focused Finish focus.
points: Naming three distinct end-of-year patterns (Limping, Striving, Focused Finish) gives teachers a diagnostic vocabulary for recognizing their own default mode rather than treating burnout or overextension as inevitable.

Stuart's own career history — quitting after year three from Limping Mode, then hitting Striving Mode during his Teacher of the Year finalist years — grounds the framework in lived consequence rather than abstract theory.
The Focused Finish resolves the tension between the two failure modes: it keeps the purpose-driven engagement Limping Mode lacks while respecting the finite bandwidth Striving Mode ignores.

Paradoxically, applying a bit more deliberate effort toward growth (Focused Finish) creates energy, while both minimal-effort survival (Limping) and maximal-effort intensity (Striving) tend to deplete it.

The fourth quarter's dual nature — rich in relational capital and experiential data about students, but also fatigue-laden — is reframed as the exact condition that makes a narrow, high-impact Focused Finish especially effective.
quotes: Limping Mode: There's a spectrum here. It can range from checked-out zombie stumbling through motions (a symptom of burnout) to the existential-question-spouting, instinctively-job-searching apostate (a symptom of demoralization).
Mere mortals fall behind as you burn forward, a blazing comet of educational intensity. This characterized years one and two of my career (now remember: I quit after the third).
The Focused Finish is how I've finished most years of my teaching career. And it's more than a small part of the reason I'm still a teacher today.
Paradoxically, using a bit more effort aimed at growth versus the bare minimum effort aimed at survival ends up creating energy rather than depleting it.

It applies the reality that you're a finite creature with a whole life outside of teaching. Instead of trying to accomplish everything (and likely sacrificing much to do so, including the quality of those accomplishments), you channel your efforts toward what you, as a professional, sense will matter the most.
